docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
The Smart Gripper we are constructing is an end-effector that uses a five-node architecture. A central Master bus node (powered by a PIC18F57Q43) coordinates telemetry from four dedicated peripheral subsystems: grip actuation, tactile force sensing, infrared proximity detection, and a 3-axis accelerometer utilizing op-amps for real-time slip detection. By continuously polling sensor data and evaluating logic states across the UART network, the master controller dynamically adjusts motor actuation. This closed-loop feedback allows the system to autonomously adjust its grip strength, ensuring it can safely secure delicate items without crushing them and automatically recover if payload slippage is detected.

  • Our team's website can be found here.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Sensor: An ADXL335BCPZ will be used to capture 3-axis accelerometer captures motion and vibration data. The three signals are then ran through high-pass filters and peak detectors by using TLV9062 op-amps before entering the micro controller's ADC (RA0, RA6, RA5).

Power Source: Power is provided through a regulated 3.3V line for the accelerometer and a 5V supply from the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano powers the signal conditioning array.

Team Connections: Connector 1 will run to our main hub (Sakiya: Board 1) which will then communicate the accelerometer slip detection data to the other boards to adjust the grip accordingly. Pins 1-4 provide digital feedback to the main control board.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Sensor: An ADXL335BCPZ will be used to capture 3-axis motion and vibration data when an object starts to slip. The three signals are ran through high-pass filters and peak detectors using TLV9062 op-amps before entering the microcontroller's ADC (RA0, RA6, RA5).

Power Source: Power is provided through a regulated 3.3V line for the accelerometer and a 5V supply from the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano powers the signal conditioning array.

Team Connections: Connector 1 will run to our main hub (Sakiya: Board 1) to send slip detection data to the other boards so they can adjust the grip. Pins 1-4 provide digital feedback and Pin 7 sends an analog signal to the main control board.

docs.title: 3-Axis Accelerometer (Slip Detection Subsystem)
docs.text:
1. Analog Devices ADXL335BCPZ 3-Axis Analog Accelerometer

    • $8.88/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Small size fits directly on our PCB without needing a separate daughterboard Very small pins make it harder to solder by hand Outputs analog signals for X, Y, and Z axes to go straight into our filters Needs extra capacitors on the board to set the filter frequency Good sensitivity for picking up small slip vibrations and in stock on DigiKey Only runs on 3.3V, so it needs a voltage regulator

  2. NXP MMA7361LCR1 3-Axis Analog Accelerometer

    • $(no info)/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Can switch between two sensitivity modes Discontinued part with no pricing or stock available on DigiKey Outputs analog signals that work with our filter design Pads are hidden underneath the chip, making it hard to check solder joints Uses very little power while running Can max out too easily if the gripper moves fast

  3. ROHM KXTC9-2050-FR 3-Axis Analog Accelerometer

    • $19.54/each
    • WinSource Electronics Product Page
    Pros Cons Direct X, Y, and Z analog outputs that work with our filter stages Most expensive option at $19.54 and only available through a third-party broker (WinSource) Uses very low power (240 uA) Tiny 3mm x 3mm package is very difficult to place and solder Filter bandwidth can be adjusted with external capacitors More signal noise at lower vibration speeds and requires a 3.3V line

  4. Analog Devices ADXL345BCCZ 3-Axis Digital Accelerometer

    • $8.01/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Least expensive in-stock accelerometer on DigiKey ($8.01) Outputs digital signals, so it will not work with our analog high-pass filters and peak detectors Has built-in tap and motion detection Requires writing extra code to read data over SPI or I2C Mounts directly to the PCB with fewer extra parts Hidden pads underneath the package are hard to inspect after soldering

Choice: Option 1: Analog Devices ADXL335BCPZ

Rationale: We need an analog accelerometer that mounts directly onto our PCB and sends X, Y, and Z signals into our high-pass filters and peak detectors. Unlike the MMA7361L (which is discontinued with no pricing) and the KXTC9-2050 (which costs $19.54 from a third-party broker), the ADXL335BCPZ is reasonably priced ($8.88) and directly available on DigiKey. It also picks up small vibrations well without maxing out when the gripper moves, and is easier to check for bad solder joints.

docs.title: Signal Conditioning Op-Amps (Filter & Peak Detection Subsystem)
docs.text:
1. Texas Instruments TLV9062 Dual Op-Amp

    • $1.24/each (3 chips needed for 6 total stages)
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Runs directly off our 5V line and uses the full voltage range for the ADC Highest cost of the three op-amp options ($1.24 each vs. under $0.50) Fast enough to catch quick slip spikes accurately Uses slightly more power when idle than slower chips Holds the peak voltage steady until the microcontroller reads it Surface-mount SOIC-8 package takes more care to solder than through-hole

  2. Microchip MCP6002-I/P Dual Op-Amp

    • $0.45/each (3 chips needed)
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Comes in an easy-to-solder through-hole package Slower response speed might miss fast slip vibrations Works on our 5V rail with full voltage output Less accurate, which can add small voltage errors across our filters Very inexpensive ($0.45 each) and low power

  3. Texas Instruments LM358P Dual Op-Amp

    • $0.33/each (3 chips needed)
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Lowest price ($0.33 each) and easy to find in stock Cuts off the top 1.5V of the signal, so we lose reading range on the ADC Easy-to-solder through-hole package Drains the peak detector capacitor too fast, making the signal drop before we can read it

Choice: Option 1: Texas Instruments TLV9062

Rationale: Each of our three axes goes through a high-pass filter and a peak detector, which takes 6 op-amp stages total. Even though the TLV9062 costs a little more ($1.24 each) than the MCP6002 ($0.45) and LM358P ($0.33), it runs right off the 5V supply from the Curiosity Nano, catches fast vibration spikes, and keeps the peak detector voltage from dropping before the microcontroller's ADC reads it.

docs.title: 3.3V Voltage Regulator (Power Supply Subsystem)
docs.text:
1. STMicroelectronics LD1117V33 3.3V Linear Regulator

    • $1.27/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Outputs a steady 3.3V and provides way more current (800 mA) than our accelerometer needs Most expensive regulator option ($1.27 each) and uses up to 10 mA just to stay on Can step 5V down to 3.3V without any issues Takes up more space on the PCB than smaller regulators Large through-hole package is easy to solder and has built-in overheat protection

  2. Microchip MCP1700-3302E/TO 3.3V Linear Regulator

    • $0.50/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Least expensive regulator option ($0.50 each) and wastes almost no power Will burn out if connected to anything over 6V Small through-hole size saves space on the board Only supplies up to 250 mA and cannot handle as much heat Works with standard 1 uF ceramic capacitors

  3. STMicroelectronics LM317T Adjustable Regulator

    • $1.13/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Can handle high current (1.5A) and wide input voltages Needs at least 5.3V input to make 3.3V, so it will not work properly off our 5V line Rugged through-hole package Almost as expensive as the LD1117V33 ($1.13) plus needs two extra resistors to set the voltage

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics LD1117V33

Rationale: Since our accelerometer needs 3.3V and our board gets 5V from the Curiosity Nano, we need a regulator that can drop 5V down to 3.3V. The LD1117V33 does this reliably without needing extra resistors like the LM317T, and its rugged TO-220 package is much harder to accidentally damage during testing than the smaller MCP1700.

docs.title: External Power Source (Power Supply Subsystem)
docs.text:
1. CUI Inc SWI12-9-N-P5 Regulated Wall Supply (via Main Hub / Curiosity Nano 5V Line)

    • $17.71/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Gives steady power (up to 1300 mA) without dying during testing Highest upfront cost ($17.71) out of the power options Easily powers the Curiosity Nano, op-amps, and 3.3V regulator Keeps the gripper plugged into a wall outlet and is not portable

  2. Tenergy 9V 600mAh Rechargeable Li-Ion Battery (30003)

    • $11.99/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Lets us test the board without wall cords and costs less than the wall adapter ($11.99) Needs an extra 5V regulator before going into the board Can be recharged instead of buying new batteries Needs a separate battery charger

  3. Energizer EN22 9V Alkaline Battery

    • $2.75/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Lowest upfront cost ($2.75) and easy to swap in for quick testing Runs out after about 4.8 hours of use and cannot be recharged Small and easy to clip onto a test board Needs a 5V regulator and turns extra voltage into heat

Choice: Option 1: Regulated 5V Supply from the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano / Main Hub (backed by the wall supply or a 9V battery for testing)

Rationale: Our board gets its 5V supply through the Curiosity Nano / Main Hub connection, which powers the TLV9062 op-amps and feeds the 3.3V regulator for the accelerometer. Even though the wall adapter has a higher upfront price, it gives us steady power when hooked up to Board 1 without worrying about dead batteries, while an inexpensive $2.75 9V battery can be used if we need to test away from an outlet.

docs.title: Section E: Battery Life Calculation
docs.text:
If running off a 500 mAh 9V battery with everything running at max current plus the 25% safety margin:

  • Battery Capacity: 500 mAh
  • Total Max Current: 104.57 mA
  • Worst-Case Battery Life: 500 mAh / 104.57 mA = 4.78 hours

To meet the requirements of creating this PCB Node, I selected the ADXL335BCPZ accelerometer, TLV9062 op-amps, and a 9V alkaline battery with a barrel jack connector. The ADXL335BCPZ beat out its competitors due to being the most reasonably priced and readily available. The TLV9062 was selected since it runs directly off the board's 5V rail. While a wall adapter is an option, having all five of our team members' boards plugged into the wall at the same time would be difficult to manage. Instead, a 9V battery with a barrel jack connector feeds into our onboard L7805 regulator to provide a steady 5V for the system while allowing mobility. From this 5V rail, a dedicated LD1117V33 voltage regulator steps the power down to safely supply 3.3V to the accelerometer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic supports a 3-axis accelerometer subsystem utilizing an ADXL335 sensor with TLV9062 op-amps for high-pass filtering and peak detection. The power management section regulates a barrel jack input down to 5V and 3.3V using L7805 and LD1117V33 regulators. System logic and data handling are managed by a PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller on a Curiosity Nano board.

Figure 1: Board 5 of Team 104's smart gripper.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The power budget for the Slip Detection Subsystem was created to verify that the power supply and regulators can support the chosen compnents in the circuit. It ensures that the L7805 5V and LD1117V33 3.3V regulators can safely power the Curiosity Nano, ADXL335BCPZ accelerometer, and TLV9062 operational amplifiers without exceeding their maximum ratings.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: The system safely operates within its limits. The total current draw on the 9V battery is 101.56 mA. The max estimated battery life of the 9V battery is 4.92 hours. Both voltage regulators have a significant overhead.
